subtitle: Store passwords safely, and make sure each user only ever sees their own data.
notes: This deck goes with exercise 4. By the end you should be able to create users with hashed passwords, refuse duplicates, and fetch only the rows a user owns.

slides.title: The big idea
slides.text:
**1. Keep passwords safe.** Never store what the user typed. Store a **hash**: a one-way fingerprint. The same password always gives the same fingerprint, but you can't rebuild the password from it.

**2. Only show people their own data.** Each note has an **owner**. The query itself keeps only Ada's notes, like `df[df.owner == "ada"]` in pandas.
slides.notes: If a database with plain passwords leaks, every account is exposed, and people reuse passwords, so their email and bank too. To check a login, Django hashes what was typed and compares fingerprints.

slides.title: The Note model you're given
slides.caption: Already written in `sandbox/models.py`. The `owner` column points at a user.
slides.code:
class Note(models.Model):
    owner = models.ForeignKey(
        settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL,    # points at the User model
        on_delete=models.CASCADE,    # user deleted -> their notes deleted
        related_name="notes",        # lets you write user.notes.all()
    )
    text = models.CharField(max_length=200)
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)
slides.notes: A foreign key is a column that points at a row in another table. Here each note points at one user.

slides.title: What the tests call
slides.caption: The tests call your three functions and pass the values in. `ada` and `bob` are users they made.
slides.code:
user = register_user("ada", "ada@example.com", "s3cret-pass!")
user.password                          # NOT "s3cret-pass!"
user.check_password("s3cret-pass!")    # True

register_user("ADA", "other@example.com", "another-pass!")
# raises ValueError("username already taken"), still only 1 user

create_note(ada, "Buy milk")    # a saved Note whose owner is ada

notes_for(ada)    # only Ada's notes, never Bob's
notes_for(ada)    # newest first: ["new", "middle", "old"]
slides.notes: Inside your functions these arrive as parameters: username, email, password, user, text. You don't create users for the tests yourself.

terms.meaning: A scrambled, one-way version of a password, like `pbkdf2_sha256$...`
The password exactly as typed. Never store this.
A column that points at a row in another table.
What `.filter(...)` gives back: a list-like set of rows.
Stop a function and report an error: `raise ValueError("...")`.
A plain function for one job, so views stay short.

slides.title: Tool: create_user
slides.caption: Creates and saves a user, and **hashes the password** for you.
slides.code:
grace = User.objects.create_user(
    username="grace", email="grace@example.com", password="tea-time"
)
print(grace.password)                    # md5$lbkk...$b9d0...  (a hash)
print(grace.check_password("tea-time"))  # True
print(grace.check_password("coffee"))    # False
slides.notes: The Console and the tests use a fast md5 hasher so they run quickly. A real project uses a slow, strong one, and hashes start with pbkdf2_sha256$. The hash is different every time.

slides.title: create vs create_user
slides.notes: Both look almost the same and both save a user. That's why this bug is so easy to miss: nothing crashes. Test 2 catches it.

slides.title: Tools: filter, __iexact and exists
slides.caption: Add `__iexact` (two underscores) to ignore upper/lower case. `.exists()` gives `True` or `False`.
slides.notes: The first filter needs an exact match, so the capital letters make it miss. __iexact is how you'd catch 'ADA' when 'ada' already exists.

slides.title: Tool: raise ValueError
slides.caption: `raise` stops the function right there. The caller can catch it with `try` / `except`.
slides.notes: The tests catch your error exactly like this and check the message. Writing return ValueError(...) instead of raise quietly hands back an error object and carries on.

slides.title: Pattern: only one owner's rows, sorted
slides.code:
grace = User.objects.create_user(username="grace", password="x")
linus = User.objects.create_user(username="linus", password="x")
Note.objects.create(owner=grace, text="Water plants")
Note.objects.create(owner=linus, text="Fix kernel")
Note.objects.create(owner=grace, text="Call mum")

print([n.text for n in Note.objects.filter(owner=grace)])
print([n.text for n in linus.notes.all()])
print([n.text for n in Note.objects.order_by("-text")])
slides.output:
['Water plants', 'Call mum']
['Fix kernel']
['Water plants', 'Fix kernel', 'Call mum']
slides.notes: Pass the whole user object: owner=grace, not owner="grace". The - in order_by reverses the order. You can chain .order_by(...) straight after .filter(...).

slides.title: Your task, step by step

steps.text: If taken (any case): `raise ValueError("username already taken")`
Swap `create(...)` for `create_user(...)` and return the user

slides.notes: Order matters in register_user: check for the duplicate before creating anything. Otherwise the duplicate is already saved and test 3 sees 2 users.

slides.title: Common mistakes
bullets: Keeping `create(...)`: "The password was stored as plain text!"
Creating the user first, then checking: the duplicate is already saved
`order_by("created_at")` without the `-` gives the oldest first
`owner=user.username`: the foreign key needs the `User` object

slides.title: Where you'll use this
slides.text: Ada opens a notes app and it calls `GET /api/notes/`. The server must answer with **Ada's** notes only, even if someone calls the API directly and skips the app.
bullets: The logged-in user is `request.user` in a Django view
Every private list filters by it: `Note.objects.filter(owner=request.user)`
Hiding data in the frontend isn't enough: the rule lives in the query

slides.title: Check yourself
questions: Why must a password never be stored as plain text?
Why check for a duplicate **before** creating the user?
